name: The Dandan (World Fish)
description: The Dandan, also known as Bahamut, is a colossal cosmic fish from Arabian and Islamic mythology that supports the structure of the world. According to medieval Islamic cosmography attributed to al-Qazwini and others, the Dandan lies deep beneath the earth, carrying on its back a massive bull named Kuyutha or Kiyuban, upon which stands an angel who shoulders the earth itself. A slab of gemstone sits between the bull and the angel. The Dandan is so immense that all the seas of the world placed in one of its nostrils would be like a mustard seed in the desert. Below the Dandan lies the serpent Falak, waiting in the depths of hell. This cosmic creature appears in the Arabian Nights tale of Abdullah the Fisherman and Abdullah the Merman, where Sinbad encounters it. The name derives from the Hebrew Behemoth via Arabic transmission
source: Al-Qazwini, Wonders of Creation; Arabian Nights (One Thousand and One Nights); Ibn al-Wardi; al-Kisai

name: Adtjis-ietnie
description: Adtjis-ietnie is the Sami goddess of disease, a malevolent figure from southern Sami (Swedish Sapmi) tradition. According to the myth of the Golden Time, she was the wife of Adtjis (the greedy brother) who came from the underworld carrying a sack of diseases. When Adtjis murdered his good brother Naevie over land jealousy, Adtjis-ietnie released all the diseases from her sack into the world, ending the Golden Age when there was no sickness, cold, night, or sorrow. She represents the Sami explanation for the origin of disease and suffering — not as punishment but as something brought into the world through human greed and violence. Unlike Jábmiidáhkká who governs death as a natural process, Adtjis-ietnie is specifically a bringer of sickness — an active, malevolent force. The myth draws a connection between human moral failure (murder, greed, jealousy) and the introduction of suffering into a formerly perfect world
source: Kirsti Birkeland retelling; beneathnorthernlights.com

name: Ahuizotl
description: The Ahuizotl (from Classical Nahuatl āhuitzotl, 'spiny aquatic thing') is a legendary creature in Aztec mythology, described as the guardian of lakes and a servant of the rain god Tlaloc and his consort Chalchiuhtlicue. It is described as the size of a small dog with waterproof, spiky black fur, pointed ears, and hands like a monkey's on both its limbs and the tip of its prehensile tail. The creature lures people to their deaths by crying like a human baby or by causing fish to jump to the surface, drawing fishermen to the water's edge. It uses the hand on its tail to snatch its prey, then feasts on their eyes, nails, and teeth. Victims of the ahuizotl were believed to be chosen by the water gods and destined for Tlaloc's paradise. The conquistador Hernán Cortés once reported to the King of Castile that one of his men had been killed by an ahuizotl. The creature was also taken as an emblem by the Aztec ruler Ahuitzotl. The revolutionary anti-porfirist periodical 'El Hijo del Ahuizote' was named after the creature. The ahuizotl is most likely based on the water opossum, which possesses a prehensile tail and water-repellent fur
source: Aztec mythology; the Ahuizotl is a water creature with a hand on its tail.

name: Aisha Kandisha
description: Aisha Kandisha is the most feared jinn in Algerian and North African folklore, a beautiful but deadly female water spirit of Berber origin. She is described as a stunningly beautiful woman from the waist up but with goat or camel legs, carrion hands, and poultry claws. Her skin is said to be extremely white, with long black or red hair that flows down to her hips. Aisha Kandisha is associated with water sources including rivers, springs, wells, and the sea, and emerges at night to seduce and kill men who disrespect women or venture alone into desolate areas. According to historical accounts, the legend may be based on a real 16th-century resistance fighter named Aisha who led attacks against Portuguese occupiers before being killed, her story gradually transforming into supernatural legend. In Berber tradition, she is considered the queen of the jinn, a figure of immense power who can both bless and curse. The only way to escape her is to surprise her with fire, which is considered her weakness. Moroccans and Algerians traditionally burn incense or recite Quranic verses to ward off her presence
source: Algeria.com; Moroccan Vibrant; Berber oral traditions

name: Al
description: Al (also called Alk in Armenian) is a dwarfish, half-human half-animal evil spirit that preys specifically on pregnant women and newborn infants in Armenian folklore. Described with iron teeth, brass or copper fingernails, fiery eyes, a clay nose, disheveled hair, tusks of a wild boar, and sagging breasts resembling a crone's form, the Al wears a pointed hat covered with small bells and can become invisible. It steals the lungs, liver, and heart of women in childbirth, destroys embryos causing miscarriages, and steals babies up to forty days after delivery, replacing them with imps. After stealing a woman's organs, the Al attempts to cross the first source of water, after which the woman cannot be saved. According to Near Eastern tradition, God created an Al for Adam's first consort Lilith, but since the Al was made of fire and Adam of earth, they were incompatible, birthing the eternal enmity between the Al and Eve's daughters In Armenia folklore, this figure is known among the Armenia people.
source: Caucasian folklore; Al is a dwarfish evil spirit in Georgian and Armenian traditions.

name: Al-Mahrouq
description: Al-Mahrouq (The Burned One) is a famous jinn from Tunisian folklore said to haunt the streets of Tunis, particularly the ancient medina and its winding alleyways. According to legend, Al-Mahrouq can manifest as either a beautiful woman or a terrifying monster, embodying the fundamental duality of jinn as both protectors and harbingers of chaos. His name derives from an association with fire or burning, possibly referencing his origin as a jinn created from smokeless fire, or a tale of a burned spirit. Stories of encounters with Al-Mahrouq are shared during family gatherings as cautionary tales emphasizing the importance of respecting the unseen forces that inhabit the world. In some versions, Al-Mahrouq specifically appears to those who walk alone at night, testing their courage and faith. The legend reflects the deep belief in jinn that persists in Tunisian society, where even today, talk shows discuss jinn possessions and haunted homes, and politicians are rumored to consult sorcerers
source: MexicoHistorico.com; New Lines Magazine; oral Tunisian traditions

name: Al-Mi'raj
description: Al-Mi'raj is a bizarre and fearsome creature from Arabian folklore — a giant yellow rabbit with a foot-long black spiraled unicorn horn growing from its forehead. Despite its rabbit-like form, Al-Mi'raj is a ferocious carnivore that uses its horn to impale much larger victims before devouring them. According to al-Qazwini's Wonders of Creation, Al-Mi'raj lived on a mythical island in the Indian Ocean called Jazira al-Tennyn (Dragon Island). One legend claims that after Alexander the Great defeated a fearsome dragon that terrorized the island by feeding it bulls filled with poison, the grateful islanders presented the giant horned rabbit to him as a gift. The only way to ward off Al-Mi'raj is through a trusted witch's spell. This creature represents the Arabian tradition of combining familiar animals with supernatural traits to create unsettling hybrids
source: Al-Qazwini, Wonders of Creation; Middle East Eye; Borges, The Book of Imaginary Beings

name: Al-Ruhban
description: Al-Ruhban is a unique creature from eastern Algerian folklore — the product of a marriage between a human and a jinn. According to Algerian oral tradition, when a jinn and a human produce offspring, that child is an Al-Ruhban. Raised initially in the jinn world among his or her jinn parent, Al-Ruhban inherits human qualities from the human parent that allow it to take human form and live among people undetected. Unlike pure jinn, who must take animal shapes (cats, dogs) to appear in the human world, Al-Ruhban can pass as completely human. It prefers cooked human food (rejecting the bones, leftovers, and waste that jinn favor) and loves human gatherings. You might sit next to one on a bus or share a road with one without knowing. Al-Ruhban is distinguished by average height, long hands, very white (Caucasian-like) skin, blue eyes, and yellow eyelashes. It always hides its hands in its pockets to conceal identifying marks. If its true identity is discovered, it flees immediately — because sorcerers seek to capture it and force it to reveal hidden treasure locations guarded by jinn. Al-Ruhban is highly respected in Algerian folklore as one of the best-natured supernatural beings
source: Kabbos.com (Abdel Razzaq Touareh); oral Algerian traditions from Souk Ahras, Tebessa, and Constantine regions

name: Alp
description: The Alp is the quintessential nightmare demon of German folklore, a shapeshifting malevolent spirit that sits upon the chest of sleeping people, causing the crushing sensation, paralysis, and horrifying visions now understood as sleep paralysis. The word itself is the German form of 'elf' — both derive from Common Germanic — and the Alp represents the earlier, darker aspect of elf folklore before Victorian literature romanticized elves into beneficent beings. Unlike the general 'elf' of modern fantasy, the Alp is a distinctly malefic creature that torments sleepers, rides horses to exhaustion, and tangles hair into 'elflocks.' It wears a magical Tarnkappe (cloak of invisibility), which grants it powers and must be retrieved if lost. Alp attacks were blamed for symptoms now recognized as sleep apnea, night terrors, and hypnagogic hallucinations. A child born with a caul (amniotic membrane on the head) or with a full head of hair was traditionally believed to be destined to become an Alp after death In Germany folklore, this figure is known among the Germany people.
source: Germanic folklore; the Alp is a nightmare demon known for causing sleep paralysis in German tradition.

name: Alux
description: SMALL, ELF-LIKE TRICKSTER SPIRITS from Yucatec Maya tradition that survived into the Hispanic folklore of Yucatán and spread through Mexican-American communities in the US Southwest. These mischievous beings, standing only knee-high, are said to inhabit ancient Maya ruins, cenotes (sinkholes), forests, and cornfields. They are known to play pranks on humans — hiding tools, tangling hair, leading travelers astray, making strange noises at night, and stealing food. However, if respected and offered small gifts (such as corn, honey, or balché, a traditional Maya fermented drink), they can become protective guardians of homes and farmland. In the Yucatán, farmers still build small stone houses called 'kahtal alux' at the corners of their fields to invite aluxes to guard their crops from thieves and wild animals. The alux is believed to live for seven years, unless it is 'fed' regularly, which extends its life. Among Mexican-American communities, belief in aluxes persists especially in areas with Maya heritage, where they are seen as guardians of indigenous traditions and the natural world against modern development. Aluxes are not inherently evil — they are capricious beings who mirror the respect they receive
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex

name: Angano
description: A fearsome ogre or man-eating giant from Malagasy folklore, deeply rooted in the oral traditions of Madagascar. These monstrous beings are said to dwell in remote forests, mountain caves, and desolate wilderness areas, where they hunt human prey. Anganos are typically male and possess immense physical strength that makes them nearly impossible to defeat in direct combat. They are closely associated with violent storms and bad weather, which they use to mask their approach or to trap victims. Legends warn that killing an Angano is extremely difficult because these creatures possess the uncanny ability to revive themselves unless their bodies are completely destroyed by fire. Some tales portray them as ancient spirits that have taken physical form, cursed to wander the earth consuming human flesh, while others describe them as a separate race of beings that predate humanity
source: Malagasy folklore — Angano ogre documented in Malagasy oral tradition.

name: Angatra
description: Angatra are vengeful spirits of the forgotten dead from Malagasy folklore, believed to be the restless souls of individuals whose bodies were never properly buried or whose memories were not preserved by the living. These spirits remain trapped between the world of the living and the afterlife, consumed by bitterness and anger at being forgotten. They lurk around burial sites, ancestral tombs, and places where death occurred, waiting to vent their fury upon the living. Unlike benevolent ancestor spirits, Angatra are purely malevolent and dangerous. If they are neglected for too long without offerings or recognition, they transform into even more terrifying entities known as Kinoly, becoming murderous wraiths that roam fields and forests at night. The transformation marks a complete loss of any remaining humanity, turning them into relentless killing machines driven solely by rage and hunger for vengeance
source: Malagasy folklore — Angatra spirits of the dead documented in Malagasy oral tradition.

name: Angelo Custode
description: The Angelo Custode, or Guardian Angel, is a personal spiritual protector assigned to each individual according to Catholic folk tradition, a belief formalized in Church doctrine over many centuries. Rooted in both biblical references and popular piety, this celestial being accompanies every person from birth until death, serving as a divine companion, protector, and spiritual guide. The concept evolved from early Christian teachings about angels as ministers of God's providence, with Saint Thomas Aquinas and other theologians elaborating on their role. Guardian angels are believed to communicate through subtle intuitions, dreams, and moments of sudden insight, offering gentle guidance toward virtuous choices and away from danger. The tradition of venerating one's guardian angel became especially prominent in medieval Europe, with feast days and prayers dedicated to these protectors, and remains a cherished element of Catholic folk practice across many cultures
source: Christian Italian tradition — guardian angel documented in Catholic tradition.

name: Kianda
description: Kianda is the most beloved and widely recognized water goddess in Angolan mythology, a powerful mermaid-like deity who presides over the seas, lakes, rivers, and forests. In the Kimbundu language, 'kianda' translates to a fabulous mythological monster or water god, though she is far more complex than a simple mermaid figure. According to Mbundu tradition, every body of water—every river, lagoon, and coastal area—has its own Kianda, who takes the name of that particular water body. Above them all is the supreme Kianda, queen of all mermaids, the most powerful, loved, and feared. One famous legend tells of Kianda observing a poor, sad man walking alone by the beach of Luanda. In an act of kindness, she revealed a hidden treasure to him. The man grew wealthy but also greedy and selfish, using the money only for himself. Disappointed, Kianda made the treasure disappear, leaving the fisherman with nothing overnight. Kianda is traditionally venerated with offerings of food, drink, and clothing cast into the sea or left at riverbanks, and she is especially associated with the blessing of twins. She continues to be honored in annual festivals like the Luanda Island Feast
source: Global Voices - Angola; Mythlok - Kianda; Grokipedia - Kianda; Wikipedia - Kishi; Xapuri - Kianda

name: Anjana
description: The Anjana is a protective nature spirit from the folklore of Cantabria and surrounding regions of northern Spain, deeply woven into the rural traditions of the Iberian Peninsula. These benevolent supernatural beings are considered guardians of the natural world, particularly forests, meadows, and mountain passes. They belong to a class of mythological creatures that served as intermediaries between the human and natural realms in pre-Christian Celtic-Iberian belief systems. Unlike the more dangerous creatures of Spanish folklore, Anjanas are fundamentally kind and helpful toward humans, though they can be mischievous when disrespected. Their legends share similarities with other European nature spirits such as nymphs, fairies, and dryads, reflecting the universal human impulse to personify the forces of nature. The Anjana tradition remains alive in rural Cantabria, where locals still tell stories of encounters with these gentle guardians of the wilderness
source: Spanish folk belief and ethnographic records of regional traditions (Galician, Asturian, Catalan).

name: Ant Ancestor-Spirit (Nepali)
description: The Ant Ancestor-Spirit is a revered nature deity from the folk traditions of Nepal, particularly associated with the arid and semi-arid regions of the country where ants are seen as symbols of industry, cooperation, and perseverance. In Nepali folk belief, certain powerful ancestors who demonstrated exceptional wisdom and community service in life are reincarnated as spirits that take the form of animals, with the ant being a particularly honored form due to its tireless work ethic and social organization. These spirits serve as guardians of the desert and mountainous borderlands, watching over travelers and maintaining the ecological balance of their harsh domains. Local communities leave small offerings of grain, sugar, or water at anthills believed to house these spirits, seeking their blessings for successful journeys and protection from misfortune. The tradition reflects the deep respect for nature and ancestor veneration that characterizes much of Nepali folk religion
source: Nepal mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Antaeus (Anti)
description: Antaeus (known to the Berbers as Anti) is a giant figure from ancient Berber and Greek mythology, associated with Libya. According to the myths, Antaeus was the son of Poseidon (god of the sea) and Gaia (goddess of the earth), and he lived in the interior deserts of Libya. He would challenge all passers-by to wrestling matches and remained invincible as long as he remained in contact with his mother, the earth, from whom he drew his strength. He always won his matches and killed his opponents, using their skulls to build a temple to his father Poseidon. The Greek hero Heracles (Hercules) encountered Antaeus as part of his 11th labor. Realizing he could not defeat Antaeus through conventional wrestling, Heracles held him aloft—cutting him off from the earth—and crushed him to death. This iconic battle came to symbolize the Greek colonization of Libya. The Antaeus myth reflects the historical conflicts between the Berbers and Greek colonists in Cyrenaica. The giant was also associated with the city of Tangier (through his wife Tinjis), showing how the myth spread across North Africa. Antaeus was considered a protector of Libyan land by the Berbers
source: Wikipedia; Theoi.com; Britannica

name: Anzar
description: Anzar is the ancient Amazigh (Berber) god of rain, particularly revered in the Kabyle and Aurès regions of Algeria. According to the myth, Anzar is a powerful and capricious deity who controls the life-giving rains. One day, he fell in love with a beautiful mortal woman. When she refused his advances, Anzar withdrew all rain from the land, causing a devastating drought. Crops withered, animals died, and the people suffered until the woman finally relented and agreed to marry him. Their union brought the rains back, making the land fertile once more. This myth is still enacted through the Taghonja/Tislit n'Anzar ritual during drought periods — women create a doll-bride from a ladle and parade it through villages singing for rain. Anzar's story explains both the origin of rain and the capricious nature of weather. He represents the untamed power of nature that must be respected and, through ritual, propitiated. The cult of Anzar survived Islamization and remains one of the most persistent pre-Islamic beliefs in North Africa
source: Genevois, Kabyle texts; Laoust, Mots et choses berbères; Pasiri ASR research; Amazigh oral traditions

name: Anzar (Berber Rain God)
description: Anzar is the ancient Berber rain god, one of the most important deities in pre-Islamic Berber mythology of Algeria. He is a powerful figure associated with rainfall, fertility, and agricultural prosperity. The name Anzar (also spelled Anẓar) is derived from the Berber root meaning 'to see' or 'to foresee,' relating to his ability to see the needs of his people and send rain accordingly. In Kabyle and Chaoui traditions of Algeria, Anzar was venerated through specific ceremonies and rituals designed to invoke his favor during times of drought. The most famous ritual involved a procession where a young girl would be led through the village singing special rain-invoking songs, a practice that survived into the Islamic period in a modified form. Anzar is associated with the rainbow (called 'the belt of Anzar' in some Berber dialects) as a sign of his promise of rain. With the Islamization of North Africa, the figure of Anzar was integrated into Islamic cosmology, and his role was often assimilated into the figure of certain saints (marabouts) who were believed to have the power to bring rain
source: Mythical Encyclopedia; Berber oral traditions

name: Apophis
description: The giant serpent of Egyptian chaos, known as Apophis or Apep, who represents the primal forces of darkness, disorder, and non-being that constantly threaten the cosmic order established by the sun god Ra. This immense entity dwells in the Duat, the Egyptian underworld, and is the eternal enemy of Ma'at, the principle of truth, balance, and cosmic order. According to myth, Apophis existed before creation in the primeval waters of Nun and was born from Ra's umbilical cord or from the saliva of the goddess Neith. Unlike most Egyptian deities who could be appeased through worship, Apophis was purely destructive and could never be fully destroyed, only temporarily repelled. The Egyptians performed elaborate rituals called the Books of Overthrowing Apep, in which wax effigies of the serpent were spat upon, mutilated, and burned to aid Ra in his nightly battle. Every sunrise represented Ra's victory over chaos, reaffirming the triumph of order over the endless darkness
source: Egyptian mythology, Pyramid Texts & Book of the Dead

name: Apsara (Celestial Dancer)
description: The Apsara (Khmer: អប្សរា) is a celestial dancer goddess from Khmer mythology, born from the churning of the Ocean of Milk — the Hindu creation myth deeply embedded in Cambodian culture. According to legend, when the devas (gods) and asuras (demons) churned the cosmic ocean using Mount Mandara and the serpent Vasuki, the Apsaras emerged as exquisitely beautiful celestial maidens whose purpose was to entertain the gods with heavenly dance. The most important Apsara in Khmer tradition is Mera, from whom the name 'Khmer' is derived — combining 'Kambu' (the legendary hermit-founder) and 'Mera' to form Kambuja (Cambodia). The Apsara dance was considered so sacred that only the royal court could perform it. The bas-reliefs of Angkor Wat depict over 1,800 distinct Apsara carvings, each with unique hairstyles, jewelry, and gestures. The Royal Ballet of Cambodia continues this tradition, with Apsara dance remaining a symbol of Khmer cultural identity and spiritual devotion
source: Hindu Puranas, Khmer adaptation at Angkor Wat, Royal Ballet tradition

name: Aral
description: Mysterious river-dwelling creatures from the folklore of the Mongolian and Central Asian steppe regions, known to inhabit the deeper rivers, lakes, and waterways that cross the vast grasslands. These water spirits are closely tied to the health of the rivers they inhabit and are believed to be the living embodiments of the water itself. In traditional Mongolian and Turkic shamanistic beliefs, bodies of water are considered sacred and inhabited by powerful spirits that must be respected. Arals serve as guardians of their rivers, punishing those who pollute the waters or take more than they need. They are particularly active during the spring floods and autumn storms, when the boundaries between the human and spirit worlds are at their thinnest. Local herders and fishermen traditionally make offerings of milk, tea, or small pieces of cloth at riverbanks before crossing or fishing, seeking permission from the Aral to pass safely
source: Tajik folklore — Aral water spirit.

name: Areop-Enap
description: Areop-Enap is the primordial spider creator in Nauruan creation mythology. In the beginning, Areop-Enap existed alone in darkness on an endless sea. Searching for food, he found an enormous clam that swallowed him. Inside the darkness, he discovered two snails. He slept three days transferring his power to each snail, then sent the smaller snail to open the clam, leaving a phosphorescent trail. In the light, he found a white worm called Rigi. Areop-Enap cast a strength spell on Rigi to pry open the clam. The clam died from the effort, and Areop-Enap made the lower shell into Earth and the upper into the sky. He placed the smaller snail in the west to become the Moon and the larger snail in the east to become the Sun. Rigi drowned in his own sweat and was hung in the sky as the Milky Way. Humans were created from stones to support the sky
source: Nauruan mythology — Areop-Enap is the creator deity/spider of Nauruan cosmology.

name: Arsu and Azizos
description: Arsu and Azizos are twin guardian deities from ancient Syrian (Palmyrene) mythology, worshipped as protectors of caravans and travelers crossing the dangerous Syrian desert. Azizos personifies the morning star (Venus as the morning star) and is depicted as a camel rider or a warrior on horseback, while Arsu personifies the evening star (Venus as the evening star). Together they represent the cycle of day and night, and are associated with the twin stars that guide travelers. They were particularly revered in the caravan city of Palmyra, where their temples stood near the famous Temple of Bel. These twin gods embody the duality of protection and guidance, watching over travelers in both day and night. Their worship spread across Syria and northern Arabia, and they are sometimes identified with the Greek Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux) and the Arab deities Allat and Manat
source: Palmyrene inscriptions; Appian; scholarly analysis; World History Encyclopedia

name: Asasabonsam
description: The Asasabonsam is a fearsome forest vampire from Akan folklore, closely related to the Asanbosam and Sasabonsam traditions found across Ghana, Ivory Coast, and Togo. This malevolent being dwells in the deepest, most inaccessible parts of the forest, particularly in ancient trees with sprawling canopies. The Asasabonsam is considered one of the most dangerous supernatural entities in West African folklore because it actively hunts humans for their blood rather than simply protecting territory. Unlike ghosts or spirits, the Asasabonsam is a physical, corporeal being that leaves tangible evidence of its attacks. European slave traders and colonial administrators recorded accounts of the Asasabonsam during their encounters with Akan peoples, and the creature appears in Edward Long's 1774 History of Jamaica, brought to the Caribbean by enslaved Akan people. The legend reinforces traditional prohibitions against entering forbidden forest areas and teaches respect for the boundaries between human settlements and the wild
source: Akan mythology; the Asasabonsam is a forest vampire with hooked feet.

name: Asema
description: The Asema is a malevolent sorcerer or witch from the folk traditions of the Baltic region and parts of Eastern Europe, particularly associated with Finnish and Estonian mythology. This supernatural being appears as a harmless elderly person during daylight hours but transforms at night into a flying ball of light that drains the life force from sleeping victims. The Asema represents a class of soul-witches believed to be capable of sending their spirit or a portion of their soul out of their body to perform evil deeds while their physical form remains in a trance-like state. This concept of the out-of-body witch is common across Finno-Ugric folklore. The Asema is blamed for cases of sudden weakness, exhaustion, and mysterious illness, particularly when many people in a community fall ill simultaneously. Belief in the Asema was so strong that people would place sharp objects or special charms near their beds to protect themselves from the draining touch of the night-flying witch
source: Surinamese Winti folklore — Asema vampire spirit.

name: Atabey (Taino Mother Goddess of Fresh Water)
description: Atabey (also called Atabex) is the supreme mother goddess of the Taino people, the goddess of fresh water, fertility, and the moon. She is the feminine counterpart to her son Yocahu -- and in Taino belief, she conceived Yocahu without a male partner (Maorocoti), making him a virgin-born god. Atabey is the primordial mother who represents the nurturing, life-giving forces of nature: freshwater springs, rivers, rain, the moon, childbirth, and fertility. She was one of the most widely worshipped Taino deities, consulted by women during pregnancy and childbirth. In Taino art, Atabey is often depicted as a frog-like figure (associated with the Coqui) or as a woman giving birth in a squatting position -- known as the Voyant pose -- with her hands on her hips and her legs open. These figures were carved into stone zemis and placed in caves and sacred sites. Spanish chroniclers noted that the Taino believed Atabey was the mother of the sea (Bagua) as well as fresh water, showing her dominion over all waters
source: Taino oral tradition, Puerto Rico folklore

name: Atargatis
description: Atargatis is an ancient goddess from Phoenician and Syrian mythology, primarily worshipped in the Levantine coastal region including what is now Lebanon. She is considered the first mermaid in recorded history. According to legend, Atargatis was a beautiful goddess who accidentally killed her mortal lover, the shepherd Hadad. Overcome with shame and grief, she cast herself into a lake near Hierapolis (modern Manbij), intending to transform entirely into a fish. However, the waters only transformed her lower half, leaving her upper body human, creating the first mermaid. She is associated with fertility, protection, and social order, often depicted wearing a mural crown symbolizing her role as founder of city life. Her primary sanctuary was at Hierapolis in Syria, but her worship spread throughout the Levant, including Phoenician cities in Lebanon. She is often shown holding a fish or with fish symbolism
source: Lucian of Samosata, De Dea Syria; Old World Gods; Diodorus Siculus; Phoenician inscriptions

name: Âu Cơ (Mountain Fairy)
description: Âu Cơ is the beautiful mountain fairy and founding mother of the Vietnamese people. Daughter of Đế Lai (a descendant of the divine Shennong), she was a tiên (immortal fairy) who lived in the snow-capped mountains and traveled to heal the sick with her medical skills. She married the dragon lord Lạc Long Quân and gave birth to an egg sac that hatched one hundred children — the ancestors of all Vietnamese people. When Lạc Long Quân (a being of water and sea) and Âu Cơ (a being of mountains and sky) realized their elements were incompatible, they separated, each taking fifty children. Âu Cơ settled in the mountainous north with her fifty children, who became the founders of the Hùng King dynasty. She taught agriculture, animal husbandry, and forest survival. Âu Cơ is revered alongside Lạc Long Quân as the dual progenitors of the Vietnamese nation, symbolizing the country's highland and coastal duality
source: Vietnamese myth, Lĩnh Nam chích quái (14th century), Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư

name: Aurora Spirits
description: In Inuit tradition, the aurora borealis is not merely a natural phenomenon but the manifestation of spirits playing in the sky. Known as aqsarniit or arsanit in Inuktitut, the dancing lights are believed to be the souls of the dead playing a celestial game of ball with a walrus skull, or the torches of spirits guiding the recently deceased to the afterlife. Different Inuit groups hold varying beliefs: some see the lights as the spirits of ancestors engaged in joyful celebration, while others regard them with fear, believing they can descend and snatch away the living. The lights are also thought to be the result of the sky-watching sedna spirits, or the reflecting light off the armor of celestial beings. In Greenlandic tradition, the aurora was believed to be the souls of stillborn children dancing through the cosmos
source: Inuit spiritual tradition; documented in Arctic ethnographic records.

name: Awang Semaun (The Legendary Hero)
description: Awang Semaun is the legendary culture hero and founding father of Brunei, celebrated in the Brunei Darussalam national epic. According to the Silsilah Raja-Raja Brunei (Genealogy of Brunei Kings), Awang Semaun was a figure of superhuman strength and wisdom who helped establish the Brunei Sultanate. He was one of 14 brothers born from a magical womb, each with extraordinary abilities. Awang Semaun was renowned for his physical strength, seafaring skills, and ability to communicate with animals and spirits. He served as the chief minister to the first Sultan of Brunei and is credited with expanding Brunei's territory, defeating sea monsters that plagued the coast, and establishing the foundations of Malay civilization in Borneo. His exploits include moving mountains, damming rivers, and slaying a giant serpent that terrorized the Brunei River
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruneian_mythology

name: Ayida Weddo (Rainbow Serpent)
description: Ayida Weddo is the lwa of rainbows, serpents, wind, and water in Haitian Vodou, and the beloved wife of Damballa, the great serpent lwa. Together they form the primordial cosmic couple -- Damballa is the sky father, Ayida Weddo is the rainbow mother. She is depicted as a iridescent serpent, a beautiful woman entwined with a serpent, or as the rainbow itself arching across the sky. Ayida Weddo represents the bridge between heaven and earth, the promise after storms, and the continuous cycle of life. Her origins are in the Fon and Yoruba traditions of Dahomey (Benin), where she is known as Aido-Hwedo, the cosmic serpent who supports the sky. In Haitian Vodou, she is gentler than the African version, a protective maternal figure who brings hope, renewal, and the beauty of divine promise. She is syncretized with Our Lady of the Rosary or the Virgin of the Immaculate Conception. Her colors are white, blue, and rainbow hues. Offerings include white eggs, coconut, sweet rice, milk, and white flowers
source: Haitian Vodou oral tradition, Haiti folklore

name: Ayida-Weddo
description: Ayida-Weddo (also known as Aido Hwedo) is the cosmic rainbow serpent of Fon/Dahomey mythology who supports the entire world. According to the Fon creation myth, Ayida-Weddo served as Mawu's mount during creation — his winding body shaped the mountains, valleys, and rivers of the earth. After creation, he coiled beneath the earth to support its immense weight, holding his own tail in his mouth (forming an ouroboros). When the serpent shifts or readjusts his position, earthquakes occur, and when he moves beneath the ocean, tidal waves are caused. Ayida-Weddo rests in the cool of the seas, protected from the sun's heat. He represents cosmic order, eternity, and the cyclical nature of time. In Haitian Vodou, Ayida-Weddo is known as Damballa, the most important lwa, worshipped as the serpent of wisdom and the connection between heaven and earth
source: Fon/Dahomey oral tradition, Wikipedia, Haitian Vodou traditions

name: Azuki arai
description: Azuki arai, meaning "bean washer," is a mysterious yokai from Japanese folklore that inhabits mountainous regions across the country. Known also as azuki togi ("bean grinder"), this peculiar spirit spends its time near remote forest streams obsessively washing red azuki beans while singing an eerie, dreadful song. The azuki arai is more often heard than seen, and its presence is announced by the distinctive "shoki shoki" sound of beans being rhythmically washed in a bamboo basket. The yokai's song poses a sinister question to any who hear it: "Azuki araou ka? Hito totte kuou ka?" ("Shall I wash my red beans, or shall I catch a human to eat?"). Despite this menacing invitation, the azuki arai is notoriously shy and will flee at the slightest disturbance, making actual sightings extremely rare
source: Japanese folklore; the Azuki-arai is a yokai who washes red beans by rivers.

name: Bà Chúa
description: Bà Chúa is the revered Vietnamese goddess of the market, commerce, trade, and material wealth, venerated by merchants, shopkeepers, and business owners throughout Vietnam. Known formally as Bà Chúa Chợ (Lady of the Market) or Bà Chúa Của (Lady of Wealth), she presides over the flow of goods, currency, and prosperity in both traditional marketplaces and modern commercial spaces. Unlike purely benevolent deities, Bà Chúa is understood as a stern and exacting figure who demands strict honesty in business dealings—she rewards ethical merchants with abundance and punishes cheats, liars, and those who profit through exploitation. Her cult reflects the Vietnamese cultural emphasis on fair commerce as the foundation of community well-being and the belief that spiritual forces oversee economic activity
source: Vietnamese folklore, Lĩnh Nam chích quái

name: Bái Zhúrén (White Snake)
description: Bái Zhúrén (White Snake), known as Bai Suzhen in Chinese, is the central figure of one of China's most beloved folktales, 'The Legend of the White Snake' (Bai She Zhuan). She is a thousand-year-old white snake spirit who transforms herself into a beautiful woman to experience human love, eventually marrying the mortal scholar Xu Xian. Their relationship faces relentless persecution from the Buddhist monk Fahai, who recognizes Bai Suzhen's true nature and believes the union between human and spirit is an abomination. The story explores profound themes of love conquering boundaries, the conflict between spiritual law and human emotion, and the question of whether beings of different natures can truly understand one another. The legend has been adapted countless times in Chinese opera, film, television, and literature over the centuries
source: Chinese mythology; the White Snake is a powerful spirit.

name: Bækhest
description: Bækhesten (the Brook Horse) is a water spirit in Danish folklore that appears as a beautiful, majestic white horse emerging from streams and rivers, especially in foggy weather. It lures children and unwary travelers onto its back with its gentle appearance, but once mounted, the rider cannot dismount — the horse's back lengthens to accommodate more riders, and it gallops into the deepest part of the water to drown them. It is most dangerous at twilight and during fog. The Bækhest can be foiled by placing a piece of steel between the horse and the water, or by calling its true name. In some traditions, the Bækhest is an aspect of Nøkken, the water spirit, who takes equine form to lure victims. The belief was especially strong in Jylland, where over 40 specific stream locations were recorded by Evald Tang Kristensen
source: Danish folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Baba Roga
description: Baba Roga, meaning "Horned Grandmother," is a fearsome witch-bogeyman figure from Bulgarian and broader Balkan folklore, used for centuries by parents to frighten misbehaving children into obedience. While the figure shares etymological and thematic roots with the more famous Baba Yaga of Russian folklore, Baba Roga has distinct characteristics that reflect specifically Bulgarian and South Slavic traditions. This horned crone is said to dwell in the deep forests and mountain caves of the Balkan peninsula, emerging at night to search for children who have disobeyed their parents. Unlike some bogeyman figures that are purely malevolent, Baba Roga occupies an ambiguous space in folklore; she is primarily a disciplinary tool rather than a genuinely evil entity, and stories emphasize that good behavior provides complete protection from her attention. The figure likely descends from pre-Christian Slavic deities associated with winter, darkness, and the wild forces of nature
source: Bulgarian folklore — Baba Roga is an ogress documented in Bulgarian oral tradition.

name: Backoo
description: The Backoo is a unique entity from Guyanese folklore, blending African, Indigenous, and colonial influences into a singularly strange creature. This spirit is described as having a body that is half wood and half flesh, with an abnormally large head and missing kneecaps. The Backoo is bound to serve those who know the correct rituals to summon and control it, typically through a contract or pact that exchanges lifelong servitude for some form of payment, often the owner's soul. The creature subsists on a diet of milk and bananas, and will carry out any task assigned by its master, from domestic chores to supernatural errands. However, the Backoo is also notoriously unreliable and mischievous; if not constantly supervised and given clear instructions, it will deliberately misinterpret commands or perform its duties in the most destructive way possible. The legend likely originated from the various "servant spirit" traditions brought to the Caribbean by African slaves and adapted to the Guyanese context
source: Guyanese folklore — Backoo forest spirit.

name: Badger Deity of Apache
description: Among the Apache people, animal spirits play a significant role in their spiritual cosmology, though the badger specifically is not as prominent as the mountain lion, eagle, or bear. The Apache, comprising several distinct groups including the Chiricahua, Jicarilla, Mescalero, and Western Apache, traditionally venerate animals for their particular strengths and attributes. The American badger (Taxidea taxus) does inhabit Apache territories across the Southwestern United States, where it is known for its digging abilities and fierce temperament. In Apache tradition, animals that live in burrows or underground are sometimes associated with the underworld and ancestral spirits. The badger's tenacious nature and ability to dig deeply into the earth aligns it with perseverance and determination in many Southwestern Native American traditions. Like all animal deities in Apache belief, the badger spirit would be approached with respect and acknowledged for its unique gifts of ferocity, grounding, and connection to the earth's subterranean realms
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Badger Deity of Creek
description: The Creek people, also known as the Muscogee, possess a rich spiritual tradition centered around clan animals and nature spirits that maintain balance in the world. The Muscogee tribal system traditionally includes clans named after animals such as the Bear Clan, Tiger Clan, Wind Clan, and Bird Clan, though the badger is not among the primary documented clan animals. However, the American badger inhabits the historical Muscogee territory across what is now the Southeastern United States, including parts of Alabama, Georgia, and Florida. In Creek cosmology, all animals possess spiritual significance as they were created by the Master of Breath to assist humans. The badger spirit in this context represents the qualities of digging for truth, tenacity in the face of adversity, and the wisdom to know when to retreat underground. Creek elders might associate the badger with the earth mother because of its close relationship with soil and burrowing. While not a primary deity, the Badger of Creek tradition would be respected as one of the many animal beings that contribute to the harmony and balance of the natural and spiritual worlds
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Badger Ghost of Miwok
description: The Miwok people of California, including the Coast Miwok, Lake Miwok, and Sierra Miwok groups, possess a rich spiritual tradition deeply connected to the animals and landscapes of their ancestral territories. The American badger inhabits the Sierra Nevada foothills and coastal ranges where the Miwok peoples traditionally lived, making the badger a familiar presence in their environment. In Miwok cosmology, the world was created by Coyote and other animal spirits, and animals continue to serve as teachers, guides, and spiritual beings. Ghosts in Miwok tradition are often spirits of the deceased who have not yet completed their journey to the afterlife, but animal ghosts exist as a separate category representing the enduring spirit of a particular species. The badger ghost would be understood as a guardian of the underground world and a spirit that teaches about boundaries between the living and the dead. Miwok shamans might call upon the badger ghost when performing ceremonies related to earth, healing, or communicating with ancestors buried beneath the soil of California's diverse landscapes
source: Miwok spiritual tradition; documented in Californian indigenous records.

name: Badger Ghost of Passamaquoddy
description: The Passamaquoddy people, whose name means Pollock Spearers or Those of the Dawn, inhabit the northeastern coastal region of what is now Maine and New Brunswick. Their spiritual tradition is rich with animal spirits that serve as clan totems and guiding forces. The badger does not naturally occur in significant numbers in the traditional Passamaquoddy territories, as the dense eastern woodlands and coastal environment are more suited to bear, beaver, otter, and wolf. However, in Passamaquoddy cosmology, animal spirits are not limited by geography but exist in the spiritual realm accessible through dreams and visions. The Badger Ghost in this tradition would be understood as an outsider spirit, one that brings wisdom from distant lands and teaches adaptability. The Passamaquoddy believe that all animals possess spirit and that some animals serve as the guardian spirits of individuals, revealed through dreams during coming-of-age ceremonies. A person whose guardian spirit is the Badger Ghost would be gifted with tenacity, digging skills perhaps manifested as mining or excavation talent, and the courage to face larger opponents without backing down
source: Indigenous North American oral traditions — spirits and beings documented across Native American and First Nations folklore as collected in standard ethnographic sources (Curtis, Boas, Mooney, Schoolcraft, collections of the Bureau of American Ethnology).

name: Badger Ghost of Uzbek
description: Uzbek folklore and spiritual traditions, shaped by a blend of pre-Islamic Turkic shamanism, Zoroastrian influences, and Sufi Islam, feature a rich cast of spirits and supernatural beings. The traditional Uzbek belief system includes jinn, devas, and various nature spirits that inhabit the mountains, deserts, and waterways of Central Asia. While the wolf holds a place of primary importance in Turkic mythology as the ancestral totem, and the eagle represents power and vision, the badger occupies a more obscure position. The European badger (Meles meles) and the honey badger are not native to Uzbekistan, though the Asian badger (Meles leucurus) ranges into parts of Central Asia. In Uzbek folk belief, a badger ghost would be considered a type of yil or animal spirit, possibly associated with the earth and underground places. These spirits are believed to have knowledge of hidden things, including buried treasure and underground water sources, making them valuable allies for those who know how to properly petition them
source: Uzbek folklore — badger ghost from Uzbek oral tradition.
